Hawaii Growth Model:
Changing Conversations about Student Performance

 Damian W Betebenner
 National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
 Dover, New Hampshire September 15th, 2016
 1

Student Growth: Introduction

• The existence of annual student testing together with
 unique student identifiers forms the foundation for the
 calculation of student growth.
• Over the last decade, most states have begun calculation of
 longitudinal student growth using large scale state
 assessments.
• The analysis of student growth is controversial because of
 the uses to which it is put: Teacher & School Evaluation.
• Development of the Hawaii Growth Model involved the
 creation of a diagnostically useful quantity that could be
 used (or not used) at a later time for many purposes.

 2

Why Student Growth?

 If you care about student
 achievement, then you care about
 student growth.

• Where you are is a function of
 where you started and how quickly
 you’ve travelled since.
• Student growth and student
 attainment/achievement are related
 in this way.
• Distance=Rate x Time
• Those who start behind tend to stay
 behind and those that start ahead tend
 to stay ahead.

 3

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and
 popular perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate student
 growth is not synonymous with understanding student growth:
 – The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple
 to understand conceptually.
 – Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult
 to calculate but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple
 conceptual basis.

 5

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• There are 3 general approaches of calculating student
 growth:
 – Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
 – Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
 – Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

 6

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Growth as an amount of change:
 – What could be more simple?
 – Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
 – Requires a vertical scale (which Hawaii has since 2015/SBAC)
 – Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
• Not as simple as it seems:
 – Comparisons between students often leads to wrong
 conclusions
 – Interpreting change requires context.

 10

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

•This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
•Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
•Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire that context.

 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age
 and is shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of
 increase—4 inches—is a well understood quantity that any
 parent can grasp and calculate at home using a simple
 yardstick. However, parents leaving their pediatrician’s office
 knowing only how much their child has grown would likely
 be wanting for more information: Parents are not interested
 in an absolute magnitude of growth, but instead in a norm-
 referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase alongside
 the height increases of similar children.

 11

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/
 student with similar characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are
 students with (at least) the same scale score history on the
 same tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for
 stakeholders to understand student growth.
• The Hawaii SGP Model (i.e., the Colorado Growth Model)
 creates growth norms for all students using regression (i.e.,
 peer-based) analyses.
• These norms allow stakeholders to understand what an
 ambitious yet reasonable expectation is for each student.
 12

Hawaii Growth Model (Student Growth Percentiles)

• Research on the SGP model began in 2007.
• Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced
 model was extended to include a criterion-referenced
 component.
• Work in other states incorporating the model into state
 reporting and accountability systems occurred in
 subsequent years and student growth became more
 common across state assessment systems.
• Goal or the model is to create an individual level growth
 metric that is informative to different stakeholders ranging
 from parents to policy makers.

 13

Hawaii Growth Model (Student Growth Percentiles)

• Different growth models answer different questions.
• Different stakeholder groups ask different questions.
• Parents are most concerned about how their child is doing.
• To effectively engage parents and communities in a
 productive conversation about student learning (i.e.
 growth), a growth model should describe:
 • What is? How much are students learning/growing.
 • What should be? How much would we like students to
 grow/learn.
 • What is reasonable? How much is it reasonable to
 expect students to grow/learn.
• Most other growth models do not provide a student level
 metric. They provide a school summary used for
 accountability purposes. 14

Growth Model: Other Options

• Almost all current growth model use large amounts of data
 to create “norms” against which student growth is judged.
• Absent large amounts of data (>1,000 grade/content area),
 professional judgment replaces large-scale data-based
 norms.
• Value-tables can be used to monitor progress of students
 between achievement bands established for year-to-year
 assessments.
• Some states (e.g., Alaska) use value-tables, particularly with
 smaller scale assessments for evaluating student growth for
 accountability purposes.

 17

Accuracy & Precision
• There was a recent report released questioning whether
 SGPs should be reported at all.
• The report questioned whether SGPs had enough precision
 to be useful for stakeholders.
• Similar to validity, precision (and accuracy) should always be
 considered in the context of use:
 • “Precise enough for what purpose”.
 • “Accurate enough for what purpose.”

 18

Accuracy & Precision

 19

Accuracy & Precision
• Infrared thermometers are precise enough for the given
 purpose.
• Educational assessment is like taking a child’s temperature:
 • You wouldn’t make a high stakes medical decision based
 solely on a child’s temperature.
 • Doctors use multiple pieces of evidence to diagnose and
 ultimately treat.
 • A child’s temperature is only useful up to a point. You
 could measure a child’s temperature to the .0001
 degree. But what’s the point????
 • High reliability/precision in educational assessment is
 often used (incorrectly) as a justification for a high stakes
 decision.
 20

Conclusions & Recommendations
• Subtraction isn’t a growth model. A growth model requires
 one consider where a student begins.
• Norms require large numbers of students. Smaller numbers
 of students requires professional judgment to decide what is
 ambitious yet reasonable progress for a student.
• Precision and accuracy of results must be balanced with
 utility: Precise and accurate enough for what purpose.
• Technical characteristics of tests and growth measures
 derived from them a often misunderstood (even by testing
 experts).
• Practical and technical issues become even more apparent
 when (high) stakes are associated with outcomes.
